source: Wason (1960) On the failure to eliminate hypotheses in a conceptual task (QJEP 12:129-140)
finding: Original 2-4-6 study read in full. Most people announced wrong rules and kept testing triples that fit them. Closes the second-hand status of the 29-person figures.
numbers: N=29 (11 first-year, 12 second-year, 6 third-year undergraduates). 6 correct at first announcement; 13 made one wrong announcement; 9 made two or more; 1 made none. Eliminative/enumerative index mean 1.79 (n=6) vs 0.24 (n=22), one-tailed p=0.0002. Mean instances before announcing: 8.0 (range 5-9) for correct, 3.68 (range 1-7) for first wrong. Second announcement: index 0.50 (correct) vs 0.19 (wrong). Tau 0.72 between eliminative index and negative-instance index.
quote: Six out of 29 subjects reached the correct conclusion without previous incorrect ones
limits: Single small sample from one lab, no sex or background effects found; index built from experimenter-coded reasons. Later work (Klayman and Ha) reframes the finding as a positive-test heuristic, not pure confirmation bias.
agent_relevance: Confirms the human anchor numbers behind G3. The useful measure is the share of tests that could be incompatible with the current hypothesis; fewer than 4 tests before announcing a rule predicts error.

source: Ragni, Kola and Johnson-Laird (2018) On selecting evidence to test hypotheses: a theory of selection tasks (Psychological Bulletin), abstract via modeltheory.org
finding: Meta-analysis of the Wason selection task. People choose instances of the hypothesis (intuition) or potential counterexamples (deliberation); framing, content and instructions shift toward counterexamples; feedback in repeated tasks makes people switch to counterexamples.
numbers: 228 experiments analysed. In 99 experiments selections were significantly more redundant (Shannon measure) than 10,000 simulations of independent selections. Model theory beat the one remaining reasoning-based theory; most of 15 rival theories eliminated.
limits: Abstract only (full paper not opened); no participant total or per-condition percentages seen. Contested: Kellen and Klauer argue the model is non-identifiable; Ragni and Johnson-Laird replied (Comput Brain Behav 2020).
agent_relevance: Feedback converts confirming choices into counterexample choices. Supports giving the agent execution feedback on its tests, not only a rule saying try to refute.

source: Sinha et al. (2025) Can Language Models Falsify? REFUTE, full text
finding: Gap 4. Execution feedback and a ReAct agent do not lift counterexample creation much. Giving the correct solution does not help either. Forcing randomized search plus brute force helps a little and finds different cases.
numbers: 324 problems after filtering. o3-mini (high): rating-implied solve 48.7%, counterexample success 8.9% zero-shot, 9.3% few-shot, 6.8% ReAct without demo, 8.6% with demo. DeepSeek-R1: solve 44.0%, counterexample 5.2/4.6/8.6/6.5. Execution feedback removed validation failures (R1 and V3 from 45 and 36 to 0) but only R1 gained in success. RandSearch: 35% of samples end in an incorrect counterexample; of those 14% validation errors and 86% wrong brute-force code. o3-mini invalidates 6% of submissions that other strategies missed (3% when given the correct solution). Dataset filter: a random generator written by Gemini 2.0 Flash Thinking without seeing the wrong code broke 58 of 403 (14%), and those were removed; 21 (6%) had planted trap constants.
limits: Competitive programming only; the kept cases were chosen to defeat random testing, so a random baseline is near zero by construction. No equal-token comparison against best-of-N. Table cells were read from layout-extracted text, so row alignment is approximate.
agent_relevance: Execution feedback fixes invalid tests but not the missing idea of what could break the code. Pair it with a random-input and brute-force generator as one S4 move, and check that the test itself is valid.

source: Ulfat, Sabit and Hossain (2026) Measuring LLM Trust Allocation Across Conflicting Software Artifacts (TRACE)
finding: Gap 6 (closest evidence). Seven LLMs judge Java bundles where faults were injected in documentation, implementation or both. Models find faults in the written spec far better than in code behaviour, and cannot reliably rank which source to distrust.
numbers: 456 bundles from 25 systems x 7 versions = 3,192 instances; 22,339 valid responses of 22,344 trials. Documentation faults detected at 67-94% (abstract; 68-95% in RQ2). Implementation-only faults: detection 21-43 points lower (mean gap 27.7). Source ranking Kendall tau_b for documentation faults 0.33 (Sonnet) and 0.30 (Opus); for implementation faults no model above 0.10. Clean false-positive rate 6% (GPT-4o) to 39% (Sonnet). Confidence separates right from wrong only for DS-V3.2 (gap 0.73). GPT-4o heavy to subtle detection 76% to 32%.
limits: Java only, temperature 0, perturbations written by an LLM (possible cues). No single per-model rate for naming the faulty artifact. Not a Duhem-Quine test with an auxiliary assumption; it is the nearest measure of blame assignment.
agent_relevance: After a failed test the agent should not guess the culprit: models trust code more than docs. Add an explicit step that re-derives the expected value independently before blaming the candidate.

source: Huang, Zhang, Harman, Du and Cui (2025, v3) Measuring the Influence of Incorrect Code on Test Generation
finding: Gap 6. When the code under test is wrong, LLM-written tests are worse; the test absorbs the code's mistake instead of checking it.
numbers: 11 models (5 open, 6 closed), 3 benchmarks, 41 repo-level examples. Correct vs incorrect code: test accuracy +57%, coverage +12%, bug detection +24%. Real-world code: tests made for incorrect code had 47% worse bug-detection rate. Adding natural-language descriptions: accuracy +18%, coverage +4%, bug detection +34%.
limits: Abstract page only; model names, relative vs absolute size of the 57%, and per-set N not read.
agent_relevance: A test written after seeing the candidate is weak. Write the test from the task text, without the candidate (G3 and S4).

source: Konstantinou, Tambon and Papadakis (2026) On the risk of coding before testing
finding: Gap 7. When an LLM writes tests after its own faulty code in the same session, the tests inherit the fault. A fresh session that sees only the task text catches more.
numbers: 5 LLMs (GPT-5-mini, GPT-4.1-mini, DeepSeek-V4-Flash, Claude Haiku 4.5, Llama 3.3 70B); HumanEval+ 164, MBPP 974, BigCodeBench 1,140. Fault detection about 14% (code first, same session) vs about 25% (test-driven, fresh session). Exposing the implementation lowers detection by 9.1 to 18.2 points depending on model; test-driven gain 7.9 to 17.7 points, mean 11.7 (all Mann-Whitney significant). Detection = test fails on faulty code and passes on reference.
limits: Same model both sides; separate-model setup not tested. Per-model gaps do not reconcile cleanly with the 14% vs 25% headline. Final N of faulty tasks not reported.
agent_relevance: Hypothesis-sampled evidence shows up in agents that write their own tests. Fix: generate tests in a fresh context from the spec, not from the candidate.

source: Batista and Griffiths (2026) A Rational Analysis of the Effects of Sycophantic AI, full text
finding: Gap 7 and numbers check. Cell values now read. The chatbot was GPT-5.1-Chat. Participants wrote the hypotheses; the AI supplied test sequences or feedback. Random sequences gave five times the discovery of default GPT.
numbers: Discovery (N=504 analysed): Default GPT 5.9%, Rule Confirming 8.4%, Agreeable 11.8%, Rule Disconfirming 14.1%, Random Sequence 29.5%. Confidence change round 1 to 3 (N=512): Default GPT +5.4 (SD 22.7), Confirming +9.5, Disconfirming -20.6, Random -56.8. Recruited 557.
limits: Humans form the hypotheses, so this is not an agent that writes its own tests. Hypotheses coded by Gemini 2.5 Flash-Lite, not the preregistered Claude Haiku 4.5; LLM-based recovery of partial data deviates from preregistration. Per-condition N not reported.
agent_relevance: Evidence from a source tied to the hypothesis does not discriminate. A source with no link to the hypothesis (random draw) did best, so random or code-generated probes are a cheap S4 baseline.

source: Jhaveri et al. (2026) Failing to Falsify, Table 2 re-read in full HTML
finding: Gap 2. Prompt changes were compared inside each reasoning mode, so mode is held fixed. Think-in-Opposites raised success in every one of 11 model-mode cells, but I:C fell in some cells. So gains are not explained by I:C alone.
numbers: Think-in-Opposites success/I:C: Qwen3-8B std 0.06/0.35 to 0.06/0.30; GPT-4o 0.11/0.25 to 0.16/0.17 (success up, I:C down); QwQ-32B thinking 0.50/0.36 to 0.59/0.37; Qwen3-14B thinking 0.34/0.19 to 0.48/0.26; Qwen3-32B thinking 0.41/0.14 to 0.61/0.54; Gemini-2.5-Pro 0.73/0.66 to 0.78/0.75. Dual-Goal raised success in 8 of 11 cases; I:C rose in 18 of 22 interventions. Thinking models emit far more tokens per turn (Qwen3-8B 8.4 vs 1088.2 at baseline). No mediation analysis, no token-matched control.
limits: One task family, 20 to 45 turns; correlation of I:C with success reported without a coefficient in the text. Length confound not ruled out.
agent_relevance: Gap 2 is partly answered: I:C is neither necessary nor sufficient for the gain. A forced step may help by making the model reconsider, not only by changing test mix. Measure both.

finding: Gap 9. Twelve models, 100 curated games. Top score is 75% and no model is near optimal. The newest listed models (GPT-5.2-Chat, Kimi-K2.5, GLM-5, MiniMax-M2.5) did not close the gap.
numbers: 12 models: GPT-5.2-Chat 75%, GPT-OSS-120B 68%, GLM-5 58%, DeepSeek-V3.1 41%, MiniMax-M2.5 35%, Qwen3.5-9B 21%, GPT-5-Nano 12%; remaining instruction-tuned models 33-35%. 100 games x 12 models = 1,200 observations (pool of 17,905 games). Spearman between success and positive-test share rho=-0.779 (p=0.003).
limits: No Claude or Gemini frontier model in the list; release dates not given; nothing tested beyond early 2026. Authors not captured.
agent_relevance: Scale alone has not removed the gap through early 2026. Keep a forced negative-test step for strong models too, but measure it per model.

source: Hamidi, Konstantinou, Degiovanni and Papadakis (2026) How effective are traditional test criteria at detecting bugs in LLM generated code?
finding: Gap 5. Planted-flaw detection by LLM-generated tests is poor. Coverage looks fine but oracles miss the bad behaviour, so passing is weak evidence.
numbers: 5 LLMs, 4 benchmarks, more than 6,000 faulty program instances, 3 criteria (statement coverage, branch coverage, mutation). Actual fault detection extremely low, often near zero. Mutation testing only marginally better than coverage at much higher cost.
limits: Abstract only; no exact percentages or model names seen.
agent_relevance: Severity must be measured by detection of known flaws, not by test count. Add planted-flaw checks when we evaluate S4.

source: Sun et al. (2026) SWE-Mutation: Can LLMs Generate Reliable Test Suites in Software Engineering?, leaderboard page
finding: Gap 5. A test-severity benchmark with injected mutants. Agent-generated test suites catch few mutants, and harder agentic mutants cut detection a lot.
numbers: 2,636 mutants from 800 instances, 7 LLMs. Agentic mutants cut mean detection from 71.04% to 39.81%. Mini-Swe-Agent: Claude-sonnet-4.5 verification 29.8%, detection 63.7%; DeepSeek-V3.1 10.2% and 36.15%; GPT-oss-120B 8% and 25.61%. Claude Code scaffold: sonnet-4.5 40.4% and 71.71%.
limits: Secondary leaderboard page (self-reported, updated 2026-06-28); arXiv 2605.22175 itself not opened. Measures test suites, not single falsification moves.
agent_relevance: A usable design: inject known flaws and score the share the test step catches (Mayo-style severity).

source: Gorman (1984) / Gale and Ball: dual-goal and disconfirmatory instruction, search snippet
finding: Snippet only: disconfirmatory-instruction subjects solved 2-4-6 more often than confirmatory and control; dual-goal instructions said to lift success from about 20% to over 60%.

source: Huang et al. snippet reading of arXiv 2409.09464 (HumanEval test accuracy 80% to 57%)
finding: A search snippet says HumanEval test accuracy falls from about 80% (correct code) to about 57% (incorrect code). The abstract says accuracy improved by 57%. The two readings conflict.
limits: Do not use the snippet number; conflicts with d05.
agent_relevance: Flagged so claims do not carry a wrong number.

source: Multi-agent assisted automatic test generation for Java JSON libraries, search snippet
finding: Snippet: LLM-made bad tests fail because of their own deficiencies (parsing errors, wrong parameters, contradictory assertions), not library bugs.
agent_relevance: Shows the test, not the code, is often the broken part, so blame needs a check.

source: LLMs as falsifiers for cyber-physical systems (listed as 2609.20752), search snippet
finding: Snippet: LLMs search for counterexamples to Signal Temporal Logic specs; reported to beat existing falsification tools on 14 of 21 ARCH-COMP specs by simulations needed.
limits: Not opened; identifier unusual; verify before use.
agent_relevance: An LLM-guided counterexample search with an exact checker can work.

source: Tian et al. 2024 LLMs for mutation testing (arXiv 2406.09843), search snippet
finding: Snippet: LLM-made mutants reach 76.47% fault detection vs 44.15% for rule-based tools on 851 real bugs.
limits: Snippet only; mutation score depends on equivalent-mutant handling.
agent_relevance: LLMs can plant flaws well enough to build a severity benchmark.
